target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels
objection: Alternative energy has not historically scaled to majority-or-near-total shares of energy demand in a large country like the U.S., where it has never exceeded about 20%, so it has not been shown to effectively replace fossil fuels at the scale large countries need.

target: AG1’s assumption that a true replacement strategy can work without continued fossil use
objection: A realistic net-zero pathway requires continued use of natural gas as a bridge fuel because existing natural-gas infrastructure can cut emissions quickly while alternatives scale; therefore, complete near-term fossil replacement is not realistic.

target: AG2’s inference from U.S. historical under-deployment to the conclusion that alternatives cannot work
objection: The fact that alternative energy has not yet reached majority shares in the U.S. does not prove it cannot replace fossil fuels, because the relevant issue is whether alternatives can be scaled and made reliable; past under-deployment in one country does not rule out future effectiveness.

target: AG2’s claim that continued natural-gas use is necessary for a replacement strategy
objection: A strategy that still depends on fossil fuels is not a true replacement strategy; if continued natural-gas use is required, then alternatives are not actually replacing fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can be a dependable quick substitute for fossil electricity
objection: Nuclear is not reliably dependable enough for a quick substitution because accidents such as Fukushima can wipe out its carbon-free electricity gains, undermining the reliability needed for full replacement.

target: AG2’s claim that nuclear accidents defeat nuclear’s usefulness as replacement power
objection: Nuclear accidents are rare and usually affect only the specific reactor or plant involved; they do not eliminate the overall low-carbon value or dependability of nuclear power for the electricity system as a whole.

target: AG2’s broader objection that nuclear’s accident risk makes it too unreliable to help replace fossil fuels
objection: Rare accidents do not erase the system-wide benefit of nuclear power, so the possibility of accidents does not negate nuclear’s role as dependable low-carbon replacement capacity.

target: AG1’s assumption that alternative energies can replace all fossil-fuel use by focusing on electricity
objection: Effective replacement must cover the full range of end uses, not just electricity, and many fossil-fuel uses—such as dispatchable power for low-renewable periods and high-temperature or transport energy—are not automatically replaced by variable renewables.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives alone can provide reliable replacement energy
objection: Variable renewable generation cannot guarantee dependable firm capacity during low-output periods, so fossil backup must remain available to preserve energy-system reliability during the transition.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can replace fossil fuels without a bridge fuel
objection: Natural gas is dispatchable and can supply electricity and industrial heat that variable alternatives cannot cover on their own, while existing gas infrastructure allows faster emissions reductions than waiting for full alternative buildout; therefore gas is needed as a bridge.

target: AG2’s claim that reliability requires fossil backup
objection: Reliability needs can be met by combining firm nuclear power with variable renewables, so fossil generation is not inherently necessary once dependable low-carbon supply exists.

target: AG2’s assumption that fossil backup must remain for reliability
objection: If alternatives can provide dependable low-carbon power over time, then keeping fossil generation for reliability is not required; fossil backup is only needed if low-carbon firm capacity is absent.

target: AG2’s claim that natural gas must remain as a bridge because alternatives only replace electricity
objection: Many fossil-fuel end uses, especially transport and residential or commercial heat, can be met by electricity or electricity-based technologies, so low-carbon electricity from alternatives can displace major fossil uses.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as a quick solution during the transition
objection: Large-scale nuclear buildout is not actually quick because it faces long lead times and significant project risk, so nuclear cannot be assumed to arrive fast enough to make fossil backup unnecessary.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can cover transition reliability without fossil backup
objection: Until sufficient firm low-carbon capacity is actually in place, energy-system reliability during the transition still requires backup dispatchable capacity, which keeps fossil generation in the mix.

target: AG2’s claim that new nuclear must be built at scale before the transition can work
objection: The transition does not require waiting for all new nuclear plants to be built; existing nuclear reactors already provide firm low-carbon power and can do so while additional capacity is added incrementally.

target: AG2’s argument that fossil backup is unavoidable during the transition
objection: If existing nuclear plants plus renewables can meet reliability needs during the transition, then continued natural-gas backup is not inherently necessary as a bridge.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables plus nuclear can replace fossil fuels without additional fossil backup
objection: AG1’s approach also requires electrifying transport and heating, which raises total electricity demand and creates new peak needs; that means substantially more firm dispatchable low-carbon capacity is required than variable renewables can provide by themselves.

target: AG1’s assumption that renewables plus existing or incremental nuclear capacity can cover all transition needs
objection: Once major fossil end uses are electrified, it cannot be safely assumed that alternative-only capacity will meet all required firm and dispatchable demand in time to eliminate fossil backup during the transition.

target: AG1’s conclusion that alternatives can replace fossil fuels without fossil bridging
objection: Because transition reliability still requires dispatchable backup and natural gas is the dispatchable option supported by existing infrastructure, a replacement strategy without ongoing natural-gas bridging cannot count as effective replacement in practice.
